This is a rebuttal to a post made yesterday. Travel to space is difficult and risky. If you run into an issue there's little you can do about it, so you'd better not run into issues.Even things as simple as food safety have massive consequences when you're far away from the nearest hospital and you need to be alert. As NASA began planning for their Apollo missions, they worked with Pillsbury to develop [Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazard_analysis_and_critical_control_points), a production monitoring process to ensure food is safe at every point.
It has since been adopted by a variety of food companies to ensure each stage is safe and if not quickly correct it rather than react to it.
I recently learned about this on [Stuff You Missed In History Class](https://www.iheart.com/podcast/stuff-you-missed-in-history-cl-21124503/episode/the-astronaut-origins-of-food-safety-105540766/). Having safer food is something we take for granted, and outbreaks are quickly identified. It all goes back to having a reason to set high standards and creating processes to meet them. Even if you don't go to space, you still have benefitted.
Of course you can point to more common innovations like GPS, but I never knew that these food safety standards were creating because of space travel. So now you know too.

Link to the paper: [https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07332](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.07332)

What's really cool here is that the angular separation of the planets is likely great enough for direct imaging to be possible with the ANDES instrument found on ELT, despite the fact they don't seem to transit. And this means we could get atmospheric readings NET 2027 when the telescope comes online.

The planets themselves orbit the dim red dwarf, GJ 1002, \~15.8 ly away, with two planets that are roughly Earth-massed. The innermost planet orbits every \~10.3 days, and is about 8% more massive, recieving about \~67% as much light as Earth, while the outermost planet orbits every \~21.2 days, and is 36% more massive, recieving about \~25% as much light.

[https://twitter.com/espresso\_astro/status/1603344597559787527?cxt=HHwWjoC-4dTanMAsAAAA](https://twitter.com/espresso_astro/status/1603344597559787527?cxt=HHwWjoC-4dTanMAsAAAA)

Actual habitability is unknown for these planets, but with so many planets being found around red dwarfs, particularly in the habitable zone (12 within 20 light years), it's worth keeping a close eye out to study these systems.

As shared in this group yesterday, the teams working with JWST on TRAPPIST-1 are gathering their data, and will have the earliest datasets (I believe) of Earth massed planets around red dwarfs, and whether or not they have atmospheres. How does it work?
1: The object has an outer layer with a higher sublimation point than the interior
2: Something causes the temperature to heat up to above the sublimation point of the interior but below that of the exterior. This is most likely to be something pushing the object to a close orbit around the parent star, but can also be caused by chemical reactions (like in a rocket), collisions or simply the geothermal heat inside the object if it is large enough.
3: When the interior sublimates, it expands. But since the outer layer is still solid, the interior material cannot expand more. Pressure builds up until the asteroid or planet explodes catastrophically (this may not destroy it depending on the circumstances. Actually something similar happens on Earth. Underground water is heated until the pressure has built up to a point where it bursts out. This is a Phreatomagmatic explosion, a type of volcanic eruption.)

text:
This is simply not true. The soviets were first to sputnik, but outside of that their firsts involved very little technical advancment over the same technology that launched sputnik. The Soviets did not have a space "program" at all like we would imagine. They had an ICBM program led by Sergei Korolev who convinced communitist leadership that "first" in space using his rocket technology could offer major propaganda wins over the western world. So they would often wait for the US to announce a launch, then race to beat them to it using risky and often poorly tested methods. The US, however was making slow, incremental steps towards all the capabilities needed for a moon landing, fairly premeditated, without much mind to intermediate milestone "firsts". 

Case in point, the soviets claimed the first to rendezvous two space craft before the US did the same in their Gemini program. It was revealed years later that they did no such rendezvous using orbital maneuvering, rather it was a simple stunt performed with matched ballistic trajectories from the ground.

 It's also worth noting that in the late 50s the USSR was already ahead of the US in ICBM development. The Russians prioritized development with their R7 program as they needed to be on par with the US in terms of nuclear payload delivery capability. The US has a geographic advantage of lots of ocean access and isolation. So by the end of WW2 the US could already leverage its carriers and bomber to deliver nukes anywhere in the world with very short notice. The USSR did not have that type of naval reach and couldn't reach the western hemisphere without investing into ICBMs.

So during the geophysical year, when scientists called for a satellite to be launched, the Russians already had the lift to put a satellite up right then and there. The US had military rockets, non-ICBM, that could put a very small satellite up, but even then, they were hesitant to do so as Eisenhower didn't want space exploration to be perceived as a military action, so he pushed back on using non-civilian rockets at first, otherwise the US very well may have been first. 

TL:DR, Russians had more capabilities at the very beginning of the space race allowing for an early headstart due to fortunate circumstances for them. The US took the clear lead though during the early Gemini Era.

Edit: this post is also very human space flight focused. When looking at LEO, the US was also the clear front runner as soon as the late 50's with respect to satellite capabilities. The USSR was a clear early leader in raw lift capabilities, but they put very little effort into satellitea past some early science instruments. The US blew them out of the proverbial water with bleeding edge tech in weather, communicatons, and spy satellite tech, hands down. But this is often lost as details thanks to th human space backdrop of the time.

text:
We know beyond a shadow of a doubt that life is incredibly rare. We just don't know precisely how incredibly rare it is. 

We do not live in a universe fine-tuned for life. Think of how little of the Earth's mass is present in any one time in the bodies of plants, animals, bacteria, and viruses. Then think of what an insignificant nothing the Earth's mass is to the Sun's. Life is clearly very rare. 

Yes, there are billions upon billions of stars, but that tells us nothing about how common life is. We know nothing about the probability of life getting started on a world. It's entirely possible that the probability of life starting on a planet is 1 in 10^100. If that were the case, Earth would be the only life-bearing world in the entire visible universe. 

And yes, we don't know that earth-like conditions are an absolute necessity for life to start and further evolve. But earth-like life is all we know, and all we can meaningfully discuss. And I wanted to write this from a very human perspective. From the point of view of humans and any kind of life form we know, these water worlds really are endless lifeless deserts. 

We know enough about life that we can meaningfully speculate about the requirements. For example, if these worlds really are just largely made of water with very little nutrients in the first several hundred kilometers of ocean depth, we have no reason to expect life to be able to thrive. There simply isn't the potential chemical complexity needed for large quantities of complex life. 

Now, you can speculate on some really exotic things. For example, it's possible that some very slow-growing bacteria could evolve on these worlds (if life can even originate in an open water column, and hydrothermal vents or similar features aren't a prerequisite.) These bacteria might evolve to survive on the vanishingly low amounts of minerals and nutrients present in the water. (There would always be some small amount present, even just the result of asteroids slowly crashing into the planet over time.) But such extremophiles are not the kind of microbes that can plausibly give rise to complex multicellular life. Large life forms like us require intricate food chains. And the slow reproduction of these extremophiles would severely impede their rise to complexity. I'm sure these bacteria would be very interesting to biologists, but these water worlds would still be nearly completely devoid of life. No complex multicellular organisms, just a few lone hardy bacteria floating around in an endless ocean. 

Yes, it is possible to imagine even more exotic lifeforms, but at some point you leave the realm of science and enter the realm of fantasy. I can speculate, "what if there were life forms made of pure water! Maybe water can somehow twist itself into complex lifeforms literally made of water!" But this is not science, it is fantasy. We have no even remotely plausible biochemistry model that might allow that. At that point, I might as well be speculating about a race of wizards who live there and stay alive through literal magic. 

Now, there are some potential and very plausible abodes for simple life in very unearthlike conditions. For example, the ice shell moons and bodies of the outer solar system could plausibly host bacterial life. But at the same time, complex multicellular life simply isn't very likely. There might be some amoebas scraping out a living in under the ice of Europa, but complex multicellular life isn't very plausible; there just isn't the kind of energy flux needed for complex food webs and the predator-prey evolutionary cycles needed for complex life. 

Yes, there may be things out there stranger than we can imagine. But from the point of view of potential homes for humans and all the life forms we would like to bring with us, the universe is very, very inhospitable. For anything even remotely like the life on Earth, the Earth really is a very rare gem.

Finally, while my words here may sound pessimistic, I hold these views really from a point of view of optimism. We know that there have to be some series of filters that prevent advanced star-faring civilizations from arising everywhere and colonizing everything. If star-faring civilizations are common, our world should have been colonized a hundred times over, long before complex life even arose. So something has to prevent that. Either life is really hard to get started, or maybe complex multi-cellular life is a rare step. Or, worst of all, maybe civilizations like ours almost inevitably destroy themselves before they can reach the stars. I personally choose to believe that we have already passed our great filters, and that despite what problems we may face with climate change, the threat of nuclear war, etc, that we will be able to survive and have a grand future beyond Earth. That life is simply very rare, and complex life even rarer still.
label: analysis

With perfect optics angular resolution is proportional to wavelength of light over diameter of the telescope: q=λ/D. Rearranging this equation allows us to determine what size telescopes we need to view an object: D=λ/q. This means that if we want to view a exoplanet the diameter of earth that is say 100 light years away we can use q = 1x10^-11 radians. If we want to view in the visible light range around λ = 500 nm = 500x10^-9 m means we need a telescope with a diameter of at least 50000 m or 50 km. The JWST has a diameter of 6.5 m. This means if we want to view a exoplanet in the visible spectrum we need a space telescope that is 10000 times larger than the JWST.

If we want to redo the calculations for the nearest confirmed exoplanet Proxima Centauri b which has an approximate angular size of 3.2x10^-10 radians we would need a telescope that is 156.25 m in diameter, or about 24 times the size of JWST

I feel like you are proving my point. There are and have been less humans well adapted to live in the Himalayas than say the temperate regions of Europe or the Fertile Crescent region of the Middle East.

So the groups who are well suited and inspired to venture outward into more extreme conditions should do so.

However, my point is a logistical point. Let’s say we have 1000 people in a village. And 3 want to go and explore an extreme region. If the other 997 think it’s a bad idea, that shouldn’t prohibit the 3 from trying. But at most they should receive 0.3% of the group’s resources in order to go explore the region.

The same situation confronts us with space travel. Those who are committed to actually doing the work and exploring should be given a proportional budget and share of the resources to do the work. Right now, I feel the % of budget and resources space travel is getting is disproportionately large compared to the amount of interest involved in actually doing the work and/or pioneering on mars, etc.

By all means, I don’t want to discourage people to try extreme things. But I also don’t want to enable them by giving them a disproportionately higher than deserved amount of resources to do so.
label: analysis
